reasoning_traces.think:
The Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm iteratively scales a nonnegative matrix to achieve a doubly stochastic form. Starting with identity diagonal matrices D₀ = E₀ = I, it alternates row and column normalization until convergence. Each iteration computes Dₖ₊₁ = diag(1/rₖ) and Eₖ₊₁ = diag(1/cₖ), where c = 1/(Aᵀr) and r = 1/(Ac). The process converges to a matrix P = DAE such that all row sums and column sums equal one. This is mathematically equivalent to solving a fixed-point problem in the space of diagonal matrices. The convergence rate depends on the structure of A, particularly whether it is fully indecomposable or positive. For positive matrices, Franklin and Lorenz provide an upper bound on the convergence factor C based on the spectral norm θ(A). When applied to web graphs, this yields a measure of page significance via the diagonal scalings D and E, which can be interpreted as node centrality scores. The algorithm's efficiency makes it suitable for massive datasets, though its performance degrades near singularities or when A loses total support.
